title: Network architecture, segmentation and tenant cell isolation
status_rationale: Unbound requirements specify tenant isolation profiles and a component monolith, but no network has been built and no hosting provider is selected.
target_answer: Unbound runs as one deployable component monolith (REQ-X-020) per deployment cell. Each cell has three network zones defined in infrastructure as code: a public edge zone that only terminates client traffic, a private application zone with no inbound route from the internet, and a private data zone holding managed PostgreSQL that accepts connections only from that cell's application identities. Production, non-production and security logging environments live in separate cloud accounts with no network path between production and non-production. Dedicated-infrastructure tenants (isolation profile C) receive their own cell and network. Segmentation is enforced by policy-as-code checks that fail the release if any data-tier resource receives a public address or an unapproved route, and an external exposure test after each deployment confirms that only the edge answers.
current_practice: Not established. No Unbound network exists. Hosting provider, regions and managed services for Unbound are not selected (no verified production infrastructure exists as of 2026-11-25).
intended_practice: Define the zone model in infrastructure as code once the provider is selected; make segmentation a release gate rather than a review item.
provable: Nothing. No production environment, configuration or operating evidence exists.
customer_statement: Unbound is pre-production. Its design calls for isolated network zones per deployment cell with the database reachable only from the application tier; this is planned and not yet implemented.
residual_risks: Network segmentation does not prevent cross-tenant access inside a shared database (profile A) or shared application process; tenant isolation there depends on application and database controls (TEN category).
Managed service endpoints (KMS, object storage, PostgreSQL control plane) are reached over provider networks whose segmentation Echelon cannot test directly.
open_questions: Which cloud provider and network primitives (virtual networks, private endpoints) will Unbound use?

Requirements disagree on the default isolation profile: CNV-ARC-001 makes schema-per-sponsor in one cluster the default while RR-UNB-PLAT-008-r1 makes a dedicated database per tenant (profile B) the default; the network design depends on which prevails.

title: Public ingress control and web application firewall
status_rationale: Edge design is a requirement-level intention only; no edge, CDN or WAF provider is selected.
target_answer: All client and partner traffic enters through one managed edge per environment. The edge accepts only HTTPS on 443, enforces the TLS policy in ECTL-ENC-002, and forwards to the application zone over re-encrypted connections. A managed WAF runs in blocking mode with a maintained rule set and Unbound-specific rules for API schema size limits; findings are logged to the security log account. Because Unbound is F# with Strata-only database access (SEC-DB-001), no user-supplied HTML (SEC-UI-001) and no application JavaScript outside Limen (SEC-UI-002), the WAF is a defense-in-depth and virtual-patching layer, not the primary control for injection or XSS. Every exposed hostname and port is declared in a reviewed ingress register; the post-deployment exposure test fails the release on any undeclared listener.
current_practice: Not established. No public endpoints exist for Unbound.
intended_practice: Select an edge and WAF capability with the hosting decision; register ingress declaratively; run WAF in detect mode during pre-production testing, then blocking mode before first customer.
provable: Nothing. No production environment, configuration or operating evidence exists.
customer_statement: Unbound has no public production endpoints yet. Planned design: a single managed HTTPS edge with a WAF in blocking mode, backed by construction-level controls against injection and cross-site scripting.
residual_risks: WAF rule sets produce false positives that can block legitimate grant or contribution submissions; tuning evidence is needed.
Construction-level rules reduce but do not eliminate injection and XSS classes (the Standard itself warns against claiming elimination without scoped evidence).
open_questions: Will Unbound process payment card data at all? If yes, PCI DSS Req 6.4.2 requires an automated technical solution for public-facing web applications, which makes the WAF mandatory rather than defense-in-depth.

challenge.customer_intent: Customers want assurance that common web attacks are blocked before they reach application code.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Exploitation of injection, XSS or deserialization flaws exposing donor PII or enabling fraudulent grants.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Signature WAFs catch commodity attacks and give virtual patching time, but are routinely bypassed by encoding tricks and do nothing for authorization flaws, which dominate in API-heavy systems.
challenge.legally_required: Not generally. PCI DSS Req 6.4.2 requires an automated technical solution for public-facing web applications only where cardholder data is in scope; that is a card-brand contractual standard, not statute.
challenge.contractually_required: Commonly expected in bank and insurer questionnaires as a yes/no item.
challenge.historical_convention: WAF became a checklist item when most web apps assembled SQL and HTML strings by hand.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Strata-only parameterized access (SEC-DB-001), no user HTML (SEC-UI-001), and Limen-confined JavaScript (SEC-UI-002) remove the main sinks the WAF is meant to guard, within the scope where those rules are verified.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Schema validation and size limits at the API boundary (SEC-DATA-001) are enforced in code on every request.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Release gates can prove the absence of string-built SQL and unsafe rendering sinks per commit, which a WAF cannot.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Construction rules plus a WAF for volumetric filtering, bot management and virtual patching of dependency CVEs.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Partly: rule enforcement evidence is per commit, but the Strata typed query interface the rule depends on was not found (see current-state brief), so SEC-DB-001 is not yet verifiable.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Unknown; unvalidated. The prior agent judgment is kept in supporting_arguments.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: Any raw SQL path, any HTML rendering of user input, or any non-Limen script would void the elimination argument for that class.
challenge.conventional_cost: Managed WAF: low setup, recurring per-request and rule-set fees.
challenge.alternative_cost: Construction controls: engineering cost already planned under the Standard; no marginal license.
challenge.alternative_risks: Over-reliance on construction claims that are not yet proven.
supporting_arguments: Elimination by construction addresses root causes that WAF signatures only approximate.
Managed WAF cost is modest, so keeping it is cheap insurance.

agent judgment: customer acceptance likelihood 'High for keeping a WAF; low for replacing it. Customers will accept the construction argument as additional depth, not as a substitute.'; institutional acceptance rating 'unlikely' (unvalidated, no cited source).
opposing_arguments: The construction controls are proposed, not implemented; today there is nothing to rely on but the plan.
Auditors and banks score WAF presence directly; removing it would create questionnaire friction regardless of technical merit.

Institutional acceptance is unvalidated: no buyer, auditor, regulator or insurer evidence or cited source supports an acceptance rating (DD-VAL-ADV-001, DD-VAL-ADV-002). Treat any rating as agent judgment until target-customer conversations or a sourced document support it.

title: Egress control and outbound connection allowlisting
status_rationale: Outbound restriction is not specified in Unbound requirements beyond provider adapters; nothing exists.
target_answer: Production workloads have no default route to the internet. Outbound traffic leaves only through a controlled egress point that permits a reviewed allowlist of destinations: payment and banking providers, custodians, charity data sources, identity provider, email delivery, AI model endpoints approved for the tenant, and cloud service endpoints (preferably via private endpoints). At the application layer, outbound calls are only possible through registered provider adapters that bind each external host to a named integration (UNB-CUST-017), so a server-side request forgery cannot target arbitrary hosts or the cloud metadata service. Denied egress attempts are logged and alerted. AI agents operating on production data inherit the same egress policy and cannot add destinations.
intended_practice: Specify the egress allowlist as data with an owner per entry; generate it from the provider adapter registry so the network rule and the code integration stay in sync.
provable: Nothing. No production environment, configuration or operating evidence exists.
customer_statement: Planned: production workloads will be denied general internet access, with outbound connections limited to an allowlist of named providers. Not yet implemented.
residual_risks: Allowlisted SaaS providers with multi-tenant domains (for example large cloud storage hostnames) can still be used for exfiltration to an attacker-controlled account on the same domain.
DNS-based exfiltration requires resolver-level controls in addition to IP or hostname allowlists.
open_questions: Which AI model providers will Unbound call from production, and will that traffic be per-tenant restricted?

title: Denial-of-service resilience and rate limiting
status_rationale: Availability and SLO requirements exist (UNB-XIN-SAS-008) but no edge, capacity or DDoS service is selected.
target_answer: Volumetric and protocol attacks are absorbed by the cloud provider's or edge provider's DDoS protection in front of the single ingress. Application-layer abuse is controlled by per-principal, per-tenant and per-endpoint rate limits enforced at the edge and again in the application for expensive operations (search, statement generation, AI-assisted features). Payment and grant submissions are idempotent (UNB-IMM-006), so retries under load cannot duplicate money movement, and the system fails closed for authoritative financial writes when it cannot commit safely (REQ-X-006). DDoS response steps are part of the incident runbook and exercised once a year.
intended_practice: Choose a DDoS-protected edge with the hosting decision; define tenant-fair rate limits so one sponsor's traffic spike cannot starve another (noisy-neighbor test in the persistence design).
provable: Nothing. No production environment, configuration or operating evidence exists.
customer_statement: Planned: provider DDoS protection at the edge plus tenant-aware rate limiting, with idempotent payment submission so load or retries cannot duplicate payments. Not yet implemented or tested.
residual_risks: Year-end giving peaks coincide with periods when attackers target charitable platforms; capacity at peak is unmeasured.
open_questions: Is a premium DDoS service with provider response team access required by any target customer, or is baseline provider protection sufficient?

title: Remote administrative access to production
status_rationale: Break-glass and operator access are specified (UNB-XIN-IAM-005, CNV-ARC-002, CNV-PLT-010); no production exists.
target_answer: There is no standing network path for administrators. No SSH, RDP or database ports are exposed to the internet or to a corporate VPN. Administrative actions on infrastructure happen through the deployment pipeline. Diagnostic access to a tenant is denied by default, granted per case with sponsor pre-approval, scoped and expiring (CNV-ARC-002), and goes through an identity-aware access broker that requires phishing-resistant MFA from a managed device, records the session and attributes it to a named person. Production database administrative roles are break-glass only with two-person activation (CNV-PLT-010); break-glass credentials are sealed, independent of the workforce IdP, expire within 4 hours and page the security owner (UNB-XIN-IAM-005). AI agents never receive interactive production access.
current_practice: Not established. No production to access.
intended_practice: Select an identity-aware access mechanism with the hosting decision; avoid introducing a VPN unless a provider constraint requires one.
provable: Nothing. No production environment, configuration or operating evidence exists.
customer_statement: Planned: no standing administrative access to production; per-case, time-limited, recorded access with phishing-resistant MFA, and two-person break-glass for database administration. Not yet implemented.
residual_risks: Provider console access by Echelon cloud administrators is itself remote administrative access and must be covered by the same controls (see CLD account structure).
open_questions: Which workforce identity provider and access broker will be used, and will break-glass credentials be held in an HSM, a sealed vault, or physical escrow?

challenge.customer_intent: Customers want to know that attackers cannot reach administrative interfaces and that administrators are strongly authenticated.
challenge.adverse_outcome: Credential theft or VPN appliance exploitation leading to direct production compromise.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: VPNs place the user on a network and then trust network location; VPN appliances have been a frequent initial-access vector (MITRE ATT&CK T1133 external remote services).
challenge.legally_required: Not by statute. NYDFS Part 500.12 requires MFA for remote access for covered entities, which flows to vendors through 500.11 policies; it does not require a VPN.
challenge.contractually_required: Some bank questionnaires still ask 'Is remote administrative access only via VPN?'
challenge.historical_convention: VPN plus jump host became the default when administration required network reachability to servers.
challenge.architectural_elimination: Immutable deployment removes most reasons to log into servers; a pipeline is the only change path.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Access broker policy can require device compliance, MFA and an approved case before a session opens.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Every session is an event with requester, approver, scope, expiry and recording reference.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Identity-aware, per-request access with no network-level trust, consistent with NIST SP 800-207.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Yes, through broker logs and the absence of exposed management ports in external scans.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Unknown; unvalidated. The prior agent judgment is kept in supporting_arguments.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: If any long-lived SSH key, bastion or database password exists outside the broker, the argument fails.
challenge.conventional_cost: VPN appliance licensing and patching burden; recurring.
challenge.alternative_cost: Broker licensing or provider-native session manager; comparable or lower.
challenge.alternative_risks: Broker becomes a high-value single point; its own compromise or outage blocks emergency work unless break-glass is independent.
supporting_arguments: Removes a well-known attack class rather than hardening it.
Produces better evidence per session than VPN logs.

agent judgment: customer acceptance likelihood 'Likely with sophisticated reviewers; uncertain with checklist-driven questionnaires that expect the word VPN.'; institutional acceptance rating 'likely' (unvalidated, no cited source).
opposing_arguments: Some examiners expect network-layer separation in addition to identity.
Break-glass outside the broker is still needed and must be just as well controlled.

Institutional acceptance is unvalidated: no buyer, auditor, regulator or insurer evidence or cited source supports an acceptance rating (DD-VAL-ADV-001, DD-VAL-ADV-002). Treat any rating as agent judgment until target-customer conversations or a sourced document support it.

title: Zero trust posture and service-to-service authentication
status_rationale: The architecture is a component monolith with one authoritative database, which limits east-west service traffic; nothing is implemented.
target_answer: Unbound does not rely on network location for trust. Every request is authenticated and authorized server-side inside the command transaction (CNV-PLT-010, SEC-AUTH-001), bound to exactly one VerifiedTenantContext (RR-UNB-PLAT-008-r1). Because Unbound is a component monolith (REQ-X-020) rather than microservices, internal east-west traffic is limited to the application, PostgreSQL, the key service and a few managed services; each of those connections uses a workload identity issued by the platform (no shared static passwords), TLS with certificate verification (ECTL-ENC-003), and least-privilege database roles. Device posture and user identity are evaluated for workforce access (END). This maps to the NIST SP 800-207 tenets without requiring a service mesh.
intended_practice: Implement workload identity for database and provider access once the hosting platform is chosen; document how each SP 800-207 tenet is satisfied.
provable: Nothing. No production environment, configuration or operating evidence exists.
customer_statement: Planned: no implicit trust based on network location; every request and every internal connection is separately authenticated and authorized. Not yet implemented.
open_questions: Can the selected managed PostgreSQL service authenticate application workloads with short-lived platform identity tokens instead of passwords?

challenge.customer_intent: Customers want lateral movement to be hard after any single compromise.
challenge.adverse_outcome: An attacker who gains a foothold moves laterally to the database or key store.
challenge.conventional_control_effectiveness: Microsegmentation reduces paths but adds rule sprawl; it does not stop misuse of a legitimate application identity.
challenge.legally_required: No statute requires microsegmentation. Federal agencies are directed toward zero trust, which does not apply to Echelon directly.
challenge.contractually_required: Questionnaires increasingly ask whether the vendor has adopted zero trust or microsegmentation.
challenge.historical_convention: Segmentation evolved for flat data center networks with many internal services.
challenge.architectural_elimination: A single deployable with in-process component boundaries removes most east-west network paths that microsegmentation would protect.
challenge.automatic_enforcement: Authorization is computed server-side for every command; tenant binding is enforced in the persistence broker.
challenge.continuous_evidence: Authorization decisions and denials are events (SOC2-002), which is stronger evidence than firewall rule exports.
challenge.stronger_alternative: Identity-based enforcement at each request plus coarse zone segmentation.
challenge.alternative_verifiable: Yes through negative isolation tests and authorization event logs, once implemented.
challenge.customer_acceptance_likelihood: Unknown; unvalidated. The prior agent judgment is kept in supporting_arguments.
challenge.invalidating_conditions: If the monolith is split into networked services, microsegmentation becomes necessary again.
challenge.conventional_cost: Service mesh and microsegmentation tooling: medium to high.
challenge.alternative_cost: Low incremental cost given the monolith decision.
challenge.alternative_risks: In-process boundaries do not stop a compromised process from reaching all components; process-level compromise is total within a cell.
supporting_arguments: Fewer network paths means fewer rules to get wrong.
Evidence is per request rather than per rule review.
agent judgment: customer acceptance likelihood 'Uncertain: some reviewers equate zero trust with specific products.'; institutional acceptance rating 'uncertain' (unvalidated, no cited source).
opposing_arguments: A single process holding all tenants' connections in profile A is a large blast radius.
Reviewers may read 'monolith' as legacy architecture.

Institutional acceptance is unvalidated: no buyer, auditor, regulator or insurer evidence or cited source supports an acceptance rating (DD-VAL-ADV-001, DD-VAL-ADV-002). Treat any rating as agent judgment until target-customer conversations or a sourced document support it.

title: DNS, domain and certificate authority hygiene
status_rationale: No inventory of Echelon-owned domains, registrars or DNS providers was located; Unbound has no production domain.
target_answer: All Echelon and Unbound domains are held in one registrar account with registrar lock, phishing-resistant MFA and at least two administrators. DNS zones are managed as code with review; DNSSEC is enabled where the registrar and DNS provider support it; CAA records restrict certificate issuance to the approved certificate authorities; dangling records pointing to released cloud resources are detected daily to prevent subdomain takeover. Workloads use the provider's resolver with query logging, and resolution of unapproved external domains from production is blocked in line with the egress allowlist. Domain expiry and certificate expiry are monitored.
intended_practice: Inventory domains, move them to a managed registrar account, and put zones under code review.
customer_statement: Domain and DNS controls for Unbound are planned but not yet in place; Echelon's current domain management practice is not documented.
residual_risks: Registrar account compromise bypasses every downstream control, including certificate issuance.
open_questions: Which domains does Echelon own, at which registrar, and who holds administrative access?
Which DNS provider will host Unbound zones, and does it support DNSSEC signing with the chosen registrar?

title: TLS termination points and visibility of decrypted traffic
status_rationale: Edge and hosting choices are open, so where TLS terminates and which third parties can see plaintext is undecided.
target_answer: TLS from clients terminates at the managed edge, which is operated by the hosting or edge provider and listed as a subservice organization. Traffic from the edge to the application is re-encrypted with TLS and certificate verification; no hop carries donor PII or credentials in cleartext. The set of parties that can observe decrypted request content (edge provider, WAF, the application) is documented in the system description. Bank account numbers and other restricted fields are additionally protected by field-level encryption at the application (ANS-ENC-008), so edge logging cannot capture them in reusable form if request logging is disabled for those paths. Edge request body logging is off by default.
intended_practice: Decide edge provider and whether any CDN that decrypts traffic is acceptable for authenticated donor traffic.
provable: Nothing. No production environment, configuration or operating evidence exists.
customer_statement: Planned: TLS terminates at a managed edge and is re-encrypted to the application; no cleartext hops. Not yet implemented.
residual_risks: A third-party edge that terminates TLS has technical access to plaintext request content, including authentication tokens.
open_questions: Will a third-party CDN terminate TLS for authenticated traffic, or only for static assets?

title: Network traffic visibility, flow logging and intrusion detection
status_rationale: Monitoring requirements exist at the application and control level (SOC2-012, SOC2-027) but no network telemetry exists; Vigila, proposed by the Standard for runtime monitoring, is a task organizer, not a monitoring system.
target_answer: Flow logs are enabled for every network in every production account and delivered to a separate security logging account that production administrators cannot alter. Detection rules alert on denied egress, connections from the application zone to unexpected destinations, database connections from any non-application identity, and traffic to known-malicious addresses using the provider's threat detection service. Missing flow log delivery is itself an alert (SOC2-027). Because most attack traffic to Unbound is encrypted application traffic, network detection complements, and does not replace, application-level security events.
current_practice: Not established. No monitoring producer exists; the current-state brief records that Vigila is not runtime monitoring.
intended_practice: Select provider-native flow logging and threat detection with the hosting decision; route alerts to the incident process.
provable: Nothing. No production environment, configuration or operating evidence exists.
customer_statement: Planned: flow logging and automated network threat detection in production with logs held in a separate security account. Not yet implemented.
residual_risks: No staffed security operations function exists; alert response capacity is unknown.
open_questions: Who will triage network alerts (in-house, managed detection provider), and with what response time?
